articles.title: Vultures are disappearing in Nigeria - but the 'Vulture King' is fighting to reverse the trend
articles.summary: Some see them as sinister or hunt them for ritual use but these birds play a vital role in nature's cycle.
articles.content:
"People fear the environment where the shrine is. No evil will ever happen here. So, nobody fights vultures that perch here," a man they call the Vulture King tells the BBC.

Mostly associated with death and decay, perhaps it is not surprising that when vultures disappeared from the skies across many West African cities, they were not missed.

Yet across the continent, their disappearance is becoming impossible to ignore, as conservationists warn that hunting linked to traditional beliefs and spiritual practices continues to threaten several vulture species to the point of near extinction.

Without vultures, ecosystems would lose a natural defence against the spread of disease.

Thankfully in one part of south-eastern Nigeria, residents are bucking the trend.

Awka-Etiti is home to a sacred forest surrounding a shrine dedicated to a deity known as Nguma.

At first glance, the site is an unremarkable cluster of tall trees wrapped in thick greenery. But at its heart stands an ancient tree that locals say has watched over the community for hundreds of years, and remains the spiritual home of the shrine.

This is a largely Christian community but some residents continue to observe traditional practices, in which vultures play a key role.

Local resident Chukwuemeka Igwe, who has earned the nickname King of Vulture, thanks to his tireless volunteer work with Nigeria Conservation Foundation (NCF), says "the indigenous don't hunt vultures".

Instead, locals sometimes offer fresh animal sacrifices at the shrine which attract the birds, he explains.

"And there is an adage we use here that says: 'When you put down a sacrifice and you do not see vulture[s], know that something happened in the spirit world'."

It means that vultures are a good omen when a sacrifice has been made because their presence suggests that the deity has accepted the sacrifice and heard the residents' appeal to its power.
articles.reasoning: The article reports on a positive conservation effort in Nigeria where local cultural practices and community leadership are helping protect vultures, a species vital to ecosystems for disease control. This has broad environmental significance and highlights a meaningful, tangible impact on biodiversity preservation.

articles.title: Lead carboxylates passivation for meter-scale perovskite solar modules
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 12 August 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-10994-7Lead carboxylates passivation for meter-scale perovskite solar modules
articles.content: Environmentally sensitive ammonium halides have emerged as indispensable surface passivators for perovskite solar cells, demonstrating broadly effective performance at the laboratory scale1-4. However, the sensitivity of ammonium halides to humidity typically necessitates operation under an inert atmosphere5. Coupled with the heterogeneous distribution of passivators during large‑area slot‑die coating, applying such surface treatment techniques to the fabrication of meter‑scale perovskite solar modules under ambient conditions remains challenging. Here, we instead employ chemically stable lead carboxylates as passivators on perovskite films engineered to have a naturally-formed formamidinium iodide-enriched surface via a high-saturation vapor pressure solvent system (2-methoxyethanol, 1,3-dioxolane, and dimethyl sulfoxide). By treating tailored surface with lead dioleate to enhance carrier transport and surface passivation, we fabricated perovskite solar modules that achieved certified efficiencies of 24.0% (aperture area of 810 cm2) and 22.0% (total area of 0.72 m2) and passed all IEC 61215 reliability tests. These results represent the highest reported performance for scalable, industrially viable perovskite photovoltaics.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant breakthrough in perovskite solar module technology, achieving high certified efficiencies at a meter scale with stable, industrially viable materials. This advancement has broad implications for renewable energy production and climate action, offering a scalable and reliable solar energy solution under ambient conditions.
articles.personality_title: New Lead-Based Coating Improves Large-Scale Perovskite Solar Panels
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Perovskite solar cells are a type of solar panel known for being efficient and cheaper to make than traditional silicon panels. However, making large perovskite solar panels that work well in normal air has been difficult because the materials used to protect them are sensitive to moisture.

**What happened** – Scientists found a new way to protect perovskite solar panels using a chemical called lead carboxylates instead of the usual ammonium halides. They treated the surface of the solar panels with lead dioleate, which is more stable in air. Using this method, they made large solar modules about the size of a small table that reached an efficiency of 24%, meaning they convert 24% of sunlight into electricity. These panels also passed important reliability tests.

**Impact** – This is the best performance ever recorded for large perovskite solar panels made with materials that can work in normal air conditions. It shows that perovskite panels can be made on a bigger scale without losing efficiency or stability. This makes them more practical for real-world use and could help produce cleaner energy more affordably.

**What's next step** – Researchers will likely work on making even larger panels and improving the manufacturing process to bring these solar modules into commercial production. They may also explore other stable materials to further improve performance and durability.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Using lead carboxylates to protect perovskite solar panels allowed scientists to create large, efficient, and stable solar modules that work well in everyday conditions.

articles.title: Best of Earth911 Podcast: The Product Stewardship Institute’s Scott Cassel on Growing Extended Producer Responsibility
articles.summary:
Revisit an influential conversation that anticipated the growth of Extended producer responsibility (EPR), the idea...
The post Best of Earth911 Podcast: The Product Stewardship Institute’s Scott Cassel on Growing Extended Producer Responsibility appeared first on Earth911.
articles.content:
Revisit an influential conversation that anticipated the growth of Extended producer responsibility (EPR), the idea that manufacturers of products and packaging should take responsibility for collecting and recycling the things they make. It was a hot topic in the sustainability and business worlds in 2023, and has become law in seven states. One EPR bill had passed in 2023, Washington State’s SB 5144, which requires battery makers to be responsible for the environmental management of their products. Meet Scott Cassel, founder and CEO of the Product Stewardship Institute, a nonprofit that advocates and consults to develop circular economy solutions and extended producer responsibility legislation. Scott and PSI were key players in the Washington legislation.

A typical concern promoted by companies about proposed EPR laws is the cost to the consumer. However, history shows that, for example, bottle deposit systems improve collection rates substantially. States with bottle bills collect 65% of bottles, while those without collect about 24% — bottle bills more than double collection rates. Columbia University research estimated a maximum increase in monthly grocery bills of $4 per household with robust EPR programs in place. The environmental benefits of EPR are clear, but the economic impact is most impressive. As part of the economy shifts to managing and moving products back to manufacturers for recycling, the Bureau of Labor Statistics projects that materials moving job jobs will grow by 6.5% by 2031, or about 861,000 new jobs. And as many as 304,000 new repair, maintenance, and waste management jobs are also expected by 2031. The Circular Economy is full of opportunity and the potential to create a more equitable nation. You can learn more about Scott and the Product Stewardship Institute at productstewardship.us.

Subscribe to Sustainability in Your Ear on iTunes and Apple Podcasts.

Follow Sustainability in Your Ear on Spreaker, iHeartRadio, or YouTube.

Editor’s Note: This episode originally aired on June 5, 2023.

This has broad environmental benefits by improving recycling rates and supporting circular economy principles. The article provides sufficient context about EPR laws, specific examples, and the role of key advocates, making it a substantive and inspiring environmental news story.

articles.title: Europe’s electric flight era could begin within four years
articles.summary:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Electric aircraft startups have been promising a lot for a long time. Two of them are now close enough to matter. Battery-electric and hybrid planes with a range of up to 500 kilometers (310 miles) would cover a quarter of Europe’s existing flight routes, according to the European Union […]
The post Europe’s electric flight era could begin within four years first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News.
articles.content:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM

Electric aircraft startups have been promising a lot for a long time. Two of them are now close enough to matter.

Battery-electric and hybrid planes with a range of up to 500 kilometers (310 miles) would cover a quarter of Europe’s existing flight routes, according to the European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA). That includes some of the continent’s most popular short hops: London to Dublin, Athens to Santorini, Barcelona to Ibiza, Nice to Corsica, and Rome to Sardinia. Every one of those routes crosses water or connects an island. Rail isn’t coming for them, which is why electrifying them is a different kind of priority than cutting routes where a fast train already exists.

The planes closest to the runway

French startup Aura Aero is building a 19-seat hybrid-electric regional aircraft with a range of up to 1,500 kilometers (930 miles), aiming for certification in late 2029. Antoine Toulemont, the company’s European affairs advisor, makes the case: “Being hybrid will help our aircraft go further, but it still cuts emissions by up to 80 percent. And it can easily use sustainable aviation fuel rather than conventional jet fuel.” The company puts the reduction in direct operating costs at 50 percent at current fuel prices.

Dutch aerospace company Elysian Aircraft, working with KLM, is developing a larger model: a 90-passenger battery-electric aircraft with a 1,000-kilometer (620-mile) range, aimed at commercial service by 2035.

The economic case is harder to ignore

The green argument for short-haul electrification has been made for years. The financial one is newer. Jet fuel prices are still volatile because of Middle East tensions, and airlines running short routes are already operating on thin margins. Carlos López de la Osa, aviation technical manager at the European Federation for Transport and Environment, puts it plainly: “Electric and hybrid flights are a core part of the solution to making short-haul travel more sustainable, and less dependent on imported jet fuel.”

In July 2026, the European Commission proposed expanding aviation decarbonization funding to cover electric aircraft development alongside sustainable aviation fuel and hydrogen-powered planes. Regulators, it seems, have stopped treating this as a distant possibility.

What the green case requires

Electric aircraft eliminate in-flight fuel burn. How green they actually are depends on what powers the grid charging them and on the emissions that go into making batteries and components. Anna Hughes, director of Flight Free UK, is direct about it: “Electric flight will be an essential part of a low-carbon world of travel. But this type of flight is only zero carbon when powered by renewables.”

That caveat carries most weight in places still running on fossil fuels. For the island and cross-water routes where electric planes are most likely to launch first, many of which already sit on cleaner grids, the math is closer to working than most passengers realize.

Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary.

The scope covers a quarter of Europe's flight routes, benefiting the general public and contributing to climate action.

**Prochaine étape** – La Commission européenne augmente les financements pour soutenir le développement des avions électriques. Les prochaines années se concentreront sur les tests, la certification et le début des vols commerciaux sur des courtes distances.

**Phrase clé** – Les avions électriques et hybrides devraient bientôt transporter des passagers sur de nombreux vols courts en Europe, réduisant pollution et coûts de carburant.
articles.personality_title_es: Europa podría tener vuelos eléctricos en rutas cortas dentro de cuatro años
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Los aviones eléctricos se han mencionado durante mucho tiempo, pero ahora dos empresas están cerca de hacerlos realidad. Estos aviones usan baterías o una mezcla de baterías y combustible para volar distancias cortas.

**Qué pasó** – La Agencia de Seguridad Aérea de la Unión Europea dice que los aviones eléctricos o híbridos podrían cubrir alrededor de una cuarta parte de las rutas cortas en Europa, como Londres-Dublín o Atenas-Santorini. La empresa francesa Aura Aero está construyendo un avión híbrido de 19 asientos que se espera para 2029. La empresa holandesa Elysian Aircraft trabaja en un avión eléctrico más grande de 90 asientos planeado para 2035.

**Impacto** – Estos aviones podrían reducir las emisiones hasta en un 80% y bajar los costos de combustible a la mitad. Son especialmente útiles para vuelos sobre agua o hacia islas donde no llegan los trenes. Esto ayuda a reducir la contaminación y la dependencia de un combustible caro que a menudo viene de regiones inestables.

**Próximo paso** – La Comisión Europea está aumentando la financiación para apoyar el desarrollo de aviones eléctricos. Los próximos años se enfocarán en pruebas, certificación y comenzar vuelos comerciales en rutas cortas.

**Resumen en una frase** – Se espera que los aviones eléctricos e híbridos lleven pasajeros pronto en muchos vuelos cortos en Europa, reduciendo la contaminación y los costos de combustible.
